Molybdos/molybdaina Pb lead is a post-Homeric name and no secure elemental lead name is attested in the Odyssey. On a strictly elemental reading copper Cu is also never named in its pure form, it is only met as the undifferentiated alloy chalkos/bronze.

The textbook statement is therefore the absence of tin and mercury as named pure metals, with iron and lead effectively un-named in the Odyssey and copper only present as the alloy chalkos. The Homeric metal vocabulary is essentially a gold-silver-bronze vocabulary.

* *chrysos* Au is named many times, *argyros* Ag is named many times,
e.g. Od. 4.73, 7.86-87, 7.129, 8.397 etc.
* *chalkos* is the metal of the age. It is the metal of weapons, armour,
tripods, cauldrons, fittings, etc., e.g. Od. 9.383 ff., 14.334, 21.11.
In Homeric usage *chalkos* is the undifferentiated bronze, the
Cu-Sn alloy.  It is not a name for the pure metal copper.

That is the whole secure metal nomenclature of the poem.  

The seven classical metals that were already handled in the
Mediterranean in the 8th-7th c. BCE, Zn and Sb excluded, are

Au Ag Cu Sn Pb Fe Hg

and the familiar non-metal S.

Of those the two canonical Homeric gaps are

* Sn tin. The Greek name *kassiteros/kassiteron* ‘tin’ is a post-Homeric
loan. Tin is of course the essential second component of Homeric
*chalkos* bronze, but the metal is never isolated and named in the
Iliad or in the Odyssey. The tin lacuna is the normal textbook statement
of the Homeric metal problem.

* Hg mercury/quicksilver. The substance is known in the Ancient Near
East and later in Greek, the later name being *hydrargyros/hydrargos*.
There is no Homeric name for a liquid silver and no elemental naming of
mercury in the Odyssey.

On the ordinary strict elemental reading the Odyssey therefore names
Au and Ag by unambiguous elemental names and it names bronze/*chalkos*
as a material. The pure metal Cu is never named in its own right, it is
only met in the undifferentiated alloy *chalkos*.

*Sideros* Fe and *molybdos/molybdaina* Pb are the next two items of the
classical list. In the Odyssey itself they are at best marginal and in
the essentially bronze-age technology of the poem they are effectively
absent as named pure elements. *Sideros* is a very rare Homeric word
and it is not securely attested in the Odyssey; *molybdos* is a
post-Homeric technical name and lead is not named as a pure element in
the poem. That is why the Odyssey is normally described as a gold-
silver-bronze epic in which Sn and Hg, and in practice Fe and Pb, are
known to the contemporary world but are not named in elemental form in
the text. If the non-metal is counted, *theion* S is likewise never
named in elemental form in Homer.

In the minimal uncontroversial formulation the elements that are
known in the 8th c. BCE Aegean world and which are certainly never
named in elemental form in the Odyssey are Sn and Hg, with Fe and Pb
being effectively un-named in the Odyssey itself and Cu only being
present as the undifferentiated alloy *chalkos*.
public_text.9:
The Homeric metal vocabulary of the Odyssey is gold-silver-bronze.

* chrysos Au is named throughout, e.g. Od. 4.73, 7.86 ff., 8.397.
* argyros Ag is named with it, e.g. Od. 7.86-87, 7.129, 4.73.
* chalkos is the normal word for the working metal of the Heroic Age, the
weapons, fittings, tripods, cauldrons etc. of Od. 9.383 ff., 14.334, 21.11
etc. In Homeric usage chalkos is the bronze alloy Cu-Sn, i.e. a single
material substance. It is not a name for pure copper in the modern
chemical sense.

On that inventory the classical 8th c. BCE elemental repertoire

Au Ag Cu Sn Pb Fe Hg

is met in the poem only as Au, Ag and bronze.

The two canonical Homeric gaps are the two metals that are essential to
that bronze but which have no Homeric name.

* Sn kassiteros ‘tin’.  Kassiteros/kassiteron is a post-Homeric loan word,
5th c. and later. Tin is present in the poem only as the unanalysed
component of chalkos. The metal is known, used and indispensable for
Homeric bronze, but it is never isolated and named in the Iliad or the
Odyssey. That is the normal ‘Homeric tin problem’.

* Hg hydrargyros ‘quicksilver’. The liquid metal is known in the Ancient
Near East and later to the Greeks, but the name hydrargyros and any
separate naming of the liquid silver is post-Homeric. The Odyssey never
names quicksilver.

On a strictly elemental naming the same practical absence holds for the
other Iron Age metals.

* Fe sideros ‘iron’ is the rare, exoticising word of the Iliad. In the
Odyssey it is at best marginal and in the usual textual census it is
effectively absent; the epic’s technology remains a bronze technology.
* Pb molybdos ‘lead’. Molybdos/molybdaina is a post-Homeric technical
term. No elemental lead is named in the Odyssey in the modern sense;
the few ‘lead’ loci that are quoted are later glosses.

Hence in the textbook formulation the Odyssey names Au and Ag
unambiguously, it names bronze/chalkos for its copper-based technology,
and it never names tin Sn and mercury Hg in elemental form. If chalkos
is read strictly as the alloy bronze and not as pure copper, pure Cu is
also never isolated and named, and in the usual strict inventory Fe and
Pb are effectively un-named in the Odyssey as well, leaving Au and Ag as
the only unambiguously named pure elements of the poem.

1.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The discussion is converging on a core Homeric metal vocabulary and a set of contested marginal cases.

Common ground:
* Chrysos = Au gold and argyros = Ag silver are unambiguously named throughout the Odyssey, e.g. Od. 4.73, 7.86-87, 7.129, 8.397.
* Khalkos/chalkos is everywhere for weapons, tools, fittings, cauldrons, Od. 9.383 ff, 14.334, 21.11 etc. The dispute is whether khalkos is a name for elemental Cu or for the Bronze-Age alloy Cu-Sn. On a strict elemental reading khalkos is bronze, not pure copper/tin.

Near-consensus absences:
* Kassiteros/kassiteron ‘tin’ Sn. No Homeric name for metallic tin. The word is a post-Homeric loan, 5th c. and later. Tin is present only as the un-analysed component of khalkos. This is the canonical Homeric lacuna.
* Hydrargyros/hydrargos ‘quicksilver’ Hg. No name for the liquid metal in the epics. The element is known in the ancient Near East but is never isolated and named in the Odyssey/Iliad.

Disputed / marginal:
* Sideros Fe iron. Colleagues 1,2,4,5,9 treat sideros as absent / marginal in the Odyssey, the epic being essentially a bronze epic and the Iliad giving iron its regular Homeric currency. Colleagues 3,6,8 cite one or two Odyssey attestations, e.g. Od. 9.391, 15... In practice the metal is at best rare and never a normal working metal.
* Molybdos/molybdaina Pb lead. Colleagues 4,8,9 claim attestations in the Odyssey for a sinker / weight / sheathing, e.g. Od. 21.11 etc. Colleagues 1,2,5 treat molybdos as post-Homeric for elemental lead and effectively absent from the Odyssey as a pure-metal name. Round 1 Colleague 10 and 7 push lead into the clear omission list alongside tin and mercury, arguing molybdos is not securely attested as elemental lead in the poem and that iron is marginal but does surface.
* Copper Cu. If khalkos is read as ‘copper’ the elemental metal is present via the bronze term; if khalkos is read strictly as the alloy bronze, pure copper is never named separately from tin.

Non-metal side notes:
* Theion S sulphur and carbon via charcoal/soot are mentioned in craft contexts but never isolated and named as elements. Colleague 10 notes charcoal is referenced, so carbon does not qualify as omitted. Sulfur remains a possible non-metal omission but the question focus is on metals.

Current working inventory of the classical seven ancient metals Au Ag Cu Sn Pb Fe Hg, with Zn/Sb excluded as per prompt:
* Definitely named: Au, Ag.
* Definitely not named as a separate element: Sn, Hg.
* Uncertain / contested: Cu via khalkos; Fe sideros; Pb molybdos.

The usual textbook statement quoted is that the Odyssey’s pure-metal vocabulary is essentially gold-silver-bronze, with tin and mercury the unambiguously unnamed classical metals, and with iron and lead effectively un-named / marginal in the Odyssey on a strict reading. Round 1 now shows a split between the canonical two-item omission Sn+Hg and a three-item omission Pb+Sn+Hg, with copper and iron/lead remaining the unresolved boundary cases.

Unresolved questions that remain for final adjudication: exact Odyssey attestations of sideros and molybdos, and whether khalkos should be counted as a name for elemental copper or only for the alloy bronze; whether lead should be counted as securely absent like tin/mercury or as marginally present.

4.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The discussion is stabilizing around a gold-silver-bronze lexicon for the Odyssey and an ~8th c. BCE known-elemental repertoire of Au Ag Cu Sn Pb Fe Hg, Zn and Sb excluded. Non-metal S is sometimes added.

Secure unanimous attestations in the Odyssey:
* chrysos = Au gold, ubiquitous e.g. Od. 4.73, 7.86-87, 7.129, 8.397
* argyros = Ag silver, ubiquitous with gold
* chalkos = the Heroic Age working metal, weapons, fittings, cauldrons e.g. Od. 9.383 ff, 14.334, 21.11. In Homer chalkos is an undifferentiated Cu-Sn alloy, bronze; the two modern constituents are never isolated and named.

Uncontested absences by name:
* Sn tin. Greek kassiteros/kassiteron is a post-Homeric loan, 5th c. and later. Tin is physically present in chalkos but never isolated and named in Iliad or Odyssey. This is the canonical Homeric tin lacuna.
* Hg mercury/quicksilver. Hydrargyros/hydrargos ‘liquid silver’ is post-Homeric technical terminology. No elemental mercury is named in the epics.

Disputed / marginal cases:
* Fe iron / sideros. Colleagues 6,7,8 cite Od. 9.391, 15.xxx etc. as attestations; colleagues 1,2,4,5,9 treat sideros as essentially Iliadic, marginal/exoticising in the Odyssey, the poem being a Bronze Age epic. Current leaning: effectively absent/marginal in the Odyssey proper.
* Pb lead / molybdos/molybdaina. Colleagues 4,8,9 cite molybdos for weights/sinkers e.g. Od. 21.11; colleagues 1,2,5,6 argue molybdos is post-Homeric and no secure elemental lead name occurs in the Odyssey. Status remains disputed, with most treating lead as effectively un-named in the poem’s metal vocabulary.
* Cu copper. On a strict elemental reading copper is never named pure, only as the alloy chalkos/bronze. On a looser literary reading chalkos is taken as ‘copper/bronze’. This reading affects whether Cu counts as mentioned.

Non-metals / incidental:
Carbon is referenced indirectly via charcoal/anthrax and soot in smithing/cooking contexts, e.g. Od. 18.175-176, 22.455-456, so it is present in narrative terms. Sulfur/theion is never named elementally.

Synthesis so far: The Odyssey’s unambiguous elemental vocabulary is Au and Ag, with chalkos standing for the copper-based technology. The textbook canonical absences are Sn and Hg. Iron Fe and lead Pb are also effectively un-named/marginal in the Odyssey itself, and pure Cu is never isolated from bronze on a strict reading. The cleanest minimal statement used by several colleagues is lead, tin and mercury as absent elemental names; the strictest maximal inventory is Cu, Sn, Pb, Fe, Hg un-named, with Sn and Hg being the unambiguously canonical gaps.

Unresolved questions remaining: the exact textual status of sideros and molybdos in the Odyssey, whether a strict count should treat chalkos as mentioning pure copper, and whether sulfur should be included in the element set.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The discussion remains anchored on the Homeric metal lexicon c. 8th c. BCE and the classical seven-metals inventory Au Ag Cu Sn Pb Fe Hg, Zn and Sb excluded.

Common ground now solidified in round 1:
* chrysos = Au gold and argyros = Ag silver are unambiguously named throughout the Odyssey, e.g. Od. 4.73, 7.86-87, 7.129, 8.397.
* chalkos/khalkos is everywhere for weapons, tools, fittings, cauldrons, e.g. Od. 9.383 ff, 14.334, 21.11. In Homeric usage it is the undifferentiated Bronze Age working metal, i.e. the Cu-Sn alloy. It is never analysed into its two modern chemical components.

Canonical, uncontested absences:
* Sn tin. The Greek name kassiteros/kassiteron is a post-Homeric loan, 5th c. and later. Tin is physically present in Homeric bronze but the metal is never isolated and named in the Iliad or Odyssey. This is the classic Homeric tin lacuna, asserted by all colleagues.
* Hg mercury/quicksilver. Hydrargyros/hydrargos ‘liquid silver’ is a post-Homeric technical term. No Homeric passage names a liquid silver/mercury metal.

Disputed / marginal items, now shifting:
* Fe iron sideros. Majority in round 1 treat sideros as essentially Iliadic and marginal/absent from the Odyssey proper; the poem is technologically a bronze world. Minority citations Od. 9.391, 15.324 are described as late/exoticising. The balance favours effective absence in the Odyssey.
* Pb lead molybdos/molybdaina. Earlier round had a minority claiming Od. 21.11 etc. Round 1 now leans strongly to absence: molybdos is post-Homeric in elemental sense and no secure elemental lead name is attested in the Odyssey. Colleague 10 and 7 now place lead in the omission list with tin and mercury.
* Cu copper. Because chalkos is normally read as bronze/alloy, pure copper is never named in its own right on a strict elemental reading. If chalkos is taken loosely as ‘copper/bronze’, copper is present only as the undifferentiated alloy.

Non-metals:
Carbon is now held to be present via charcoal/anthrax and soot in smithing/cooking contexts, e.g. Od. 18.175-176, 22.455-456, so it is not counted as omitted. Sulphur/theion is never named in elemental form; discussion is peripheral as the question is focused on metals.

Current synthesis:
Definitely unmentioned in elemental name in the Odyssey are Sn tin and Hg mercury. With a strict elemental reading Cu copper is also unmentioned as a pure metal, being covered only by the alloy term chalkos. Fe iron and Pb lead are the most contested but round 1 majority now treats them as effectively un-named/marginal in the Odyssey itself. The textbook minimal formulation is Au and Ag named, bronze/chalkos present, and the two classical metals already in use in the 8th c. Mediterranean but with no Homeric elemental name are Sn and Hg, with Fe and Pb effectively absent in the Odyssey and Cu absent in pure form on a strict reading. Unresolved remains how strictly to count chalkos as copper and whether any secure Odyssey attestation of sideros or molybdos exists; the non-metal scope of the question also remains open.

* Sn tin. The Greek name kassiteros/kassiteron is post-Homeric, 5th c. and later. Tin is physically present in Homeric bronze but the metal is never isolated and named in Iliad or Odyssey. This is the canonical Homeric tin lacuna.

Colleagues 4,8,9 cite molybdos in Od. 21.11 etc. for weights/sinkers. Colleague 10 now lists lead as a clean omission alongside tin and mercury. The lexical dating remains disputed.

In unambiguous elemental naming the Odyssey gives Au and Ag. Sn and Hg are the canonical, unambiguously un-named classical metals. Fe and Pb are effectively un-named/marginal in the Odyssey proper, with Fe being the more disputed of the two. Cu is absent in pure form if chalkos is read strictly as alloy. The maximally strict un-named ancient elemental repertoire in the Odyssey is Cu, Sn, Pb, Fe, Hg; the minimal uncontroversial formulation repeatedly quoted is Sn and Hg, with many colleagues adding Pb as a third secure omission and treating Fe as marginal/late. Iron attestations and the status of molybdos in Od. 21.11 remain the unresolved points.

5.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The discussion is converging on a core of secure mentions and a set of canonical absences, with persistent disputes on iron, lead and the status of chalkos.

Agreed core mentions:
* chrysos = Au gold repeatedly named, e.g. Od. 4.73, 7.86 ff, 8.397.
* argyros = Ag silver repeatedly named with gold, e.g. Od. 7.86-87, 7.129, 4.73.
* chalkos/khalkos is everywhere as the heroic working metal, weapons, tripods, cauldrons, Od. 9.383 ff, 14.334, 21.11 etc. The dispute is its chemical reading: Colleagues 1,2,5,6,8 treat chalkos strictly as bronze Cu-Sn alloy, so pure copper is never isolated by name; Colleagues 3,4,7,9 treat chalkos as the Homeric name for copper/bronze, i.e. the copper element is present in the vocabulary.

Canonical uncontested absences by name:
* Sn tin. Kassiteros/kassiteron ‘tin’ is a post-Homeric loan, 5th c. and later. Tin is physically present in Homeric bronze but the metal is never named in its own right in Iliad or Odyssey. This is the textbook Homeric tin problem, now unanimous in round 1.
* Hg mercury/quicksilver. Hydrargyros/hydrargos ‘quicksilver’ is post-Homeric technical term. No separate naming of liquid silver occurs in the epics. Unanimous.

Disputed/marginal metals:
* Fe iron sideros. Colleagues 1,2,5,8 say sideros is very rare in Homer and absent/effectively absent from Odyssey; the epic is essentially Bronze Age. Colleagues 6,8 cite Od. 9.391, 15... as attestations and claim iron is present albeit marginal. Colleague 3,4,9 say sideros occurs in few Homeric iron references but is marginal/exoticising in Odyssey. Unresolved whether any genuine Odyssey citation is secure.
* Pb lead molybdos/molybdaina. Colleague 4 and 9 claim Odyssey names lead molubdos Od.21.11 etc., and molybdos for weights/sinkers. Colleagues 1,2,5,8,10 say molybdos is post-Homeric and elemental lead is not named in Odyssey; any references are late glosses/interpretations. Colleague 10 now explicitly lists lead as absent with tin and mercury. Disagreement persists on lexical attestation.
* Cu copper. Depends on interpretation of chalkos. Strict elemental reading → copper is never named pure, only as alloy bronze. Loose reading → chalkos = copper/bronze.

Non-metal elements:
* Carbon is referenced indirectly via charcoal/anthrax, e.g. Od. 18.175-176, 22.455-456, so colleagues 7,10 argue it should not be counted as omitted.
* Sulphur/theion S is repeatedly cited as never named in elemental sense; Colleague 7 lists it as omitted, Colleague 3,8 note theion is not Homeric. Question focus is unclear whether non-metals are in scope.

Current working inventory of classical metals known in elemental form c.800 BCE, excluding Zn and Sb: Au, Ag, Cu, Sn, Pb, Fe, Hg.

Best supported omissions on strict naming basis: Sn and Hg definitely un-named. Fe and Pb are effectively un-named/marginal in Odyssey in most accounts, with iron the more contested. Cu pure is un-named on strict alloy reading.

Unresolved questions for next round: exact Odyssey citations for sideros and molybdos and their textual security; whether chalkos should be counted as pure copper; whether the question’s “elements known” set should be limited to the seven ancient metals or also include non-metals such as sulphur/carbon; how to treat the traditional “gold-silver-bronze” canon versus a maximal elemental list Cu, Sn, Pb, Fe, Hg as unmentioned.

My belief is shifting toward the textbook formulation: Au and Ag unambiguously named; chalkos = bronze; canonical named absences Sn and Hg, with Fe and Pb effectively absent in Odyssey and Cu absent in pure form on strict reading, with lead the most contested of those.

6.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The deliberation is converging on a gold–silver–chalkos core with a canonical tin/mercury lacuna, but the status of iron, lead and pure copper in the Odyssey remains disputed.

Consensus points that now hold across most colleagues:
* chrysos Au gold and argyros Ag silver are unambiguously named many times, e.g. Od. 4.73, 7.86-87, 7.129, 8.397 etc.
* khalkos/chalkos is ubiquitous for weapons, tools, fittings, cauldrons, Od. 9.383 ff, 14.334, 21.11 etc. In Homer it is the undifferentiated working metal of the Bronze Age, i.e. the Cu-Sn alloy. Whether this is read as ‘copper/bronze’ in literary shorthand or strictly as bronze is the crux for Cu.
* Kassiteros/kassiteron ‘tin’ Sn is never a Homeric word; it is a post-Homeric 5th c. and later loan. Tin is physically present in Homeric bronze but never named as a separate pure metal. That is the textbook Homeric tin problem.
* Hydrargyros/hydrargos ‘quicksilver/mercury’ Hg is never named in the epics; the name is post-Homeric technical terminology.

Disagreements / nuance updated from round 1:
* Iron sideros Fe. Colleagues 1,2,4,5,6,8 argue sideros is essentially Iliadic, marginal/exoticising and effectively absent from the Odyssey; Colleagues 6,7,9 cite Odyssey attestations e.g. Od. 9.391, 15.324 etc. The poem is technologically bronze-age; even if an occurrence exists it is rare.
* Lead molybdos/molybdaina Pb. Colleagues 1,2,5,6 say the elemental name is post-Homeric and lead is effectively absent as a named pure element in the Odyssey. Colleagues 4,8,9 cite Molubdos at Od. 21.11 and fishing-weight/sinker uses. Lexical dating of molybdos is contested and the passage is often read as a later gloss.
* Copper Cu. If chalkos is taken strictly as the alloy bronze Cu-Sn, pure copper is never named in its own right, only the alloy. Colleagues 2,5,6,8,9 hold this strict reading; others treat chalkos as the Homeric copper/bronze metal and count copper as present.
* Non-metals. Sulphur theion S is not a Homeric word and is never named elementally; carbon is referenced indirectly via anthrax charcoal/soot, e.g. Od. 18.175-176, 22.455-456, so Colleague 10 argues carbon should not be counted as omitted. The question’s focus is usually on the seven classical metals Au Ag Cu Sn Pb Fe Hg with Zn and Sb excluded.

Current working picture:
Uncontroversially absent by name are tin Sn and mercury Hg. Lead Pb and iron Fe are the marginal cases: the strongest majority testimony in the current round still favours their effective absence or marginality in the Odyssey proper, with lead being the more contested because of Od. 21.11. Copper as a pure element is absent on a strict elemental reading; on the looser literary reading copper is present via chalkos.

Unresolved questions that will matter for the final list:
* Exact textual status of sideros in the Odyssey and whether any attestation is secure and non-glossed.
* Whether molubdos at Od. 21.11 is a secure elemental lead name or a later interpretation.
* Whether the question requires a strict chemical-element reading where chalkos = bronze ⇒ Cu un-named, or a literary reading where chalkos = copper/bronze ⇒ Cu named.
* Whether sulphur/carbon should be counted in the “elements known in elemental form” inventory.

The classic scholarly formulation most often cited remains: Odyssey pure-metal vocabulary is essentially gold and silver, with bronze/chalkos for the copper-based technology, and the canonical un-named classical metals are tin Sn and quicksilver Hg, with iron Fe and lead Pb effectively un-named/marginal in the Odyssey itself.

8.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The discussion is converging on a small Homeric metal vocabulary with a large disputed periphery.

Elements that are uncontroversial in the Odyssey:
* chrysos = Au gold is named repeatedly, e.g. Od. 4.73, 7.86ff, 8.397
* argyros = Ag silver is named repeatedly with it, e.g. Od. 7.86-87, 7.129, 4.73
* chalkos is everywhere for weapons, tools, fittings, cauldrons, e.g. Od. 9.383 ff, 14.334, 21.11. Consensus is that in Homer chalkos is the Bronze Age working metal, i.e. bronze as a single substance, not an analytical Cu-Sn alloy. Whether that counts as a naming of pure Cu is contested.

Classical seven metals available c.8th c. BCE, Zn and Sb excluded: Au, Ag, Cu, Sn, Pb, Fe, Hg.

Uncontested gaps by name:
* Sn tin. The Greek name kassiteros/kassiteron for metallic tin is post-Homeric, 5th c.–later. Tin is present in Homeric bronze but is never isolated and named in the Iliad or Odyssey. This is the textbook Homeric tin gap.
* Hg mercury/quicksilver. Hydrargyros / hydrargos is post-Homeric technical terminology. No Homeric passage names liquid silver/mercury as an element. Hermes is present, the metal is not.

Disputed core:
* Fe sideros iron. Colleague 1,2,4,5,6,8,9 argue sideros is rare in Homer and effectively absent from the Odyssey; the epic remains a Bronze Age epic and iron is marginal/late, with the Iliad providing the regular Homeric currency. Colleague 3,4,6,8,9 note a few Odyssey citations such as Od. 9.391, 15.324 etc. but these are described as late / exoticising. Colleague 7/10 claim iron is named.
* Pb lead. Molybdos/molybdaina for lead is described as post-Homeric in several accounts and the Odyssey shows no reliable elemental lead naming. Colleague 3,4,8,9 claim attestations e.g. Od. 21.11 for lead and for weights/sinkers. Colleague 1,2,5,6,8 argue any Odyssey ‘molybd-’ references are late scholia/interpretations and the metal is not named as a pure element in the poem’s own nomenclature.

Cu ambiguity:
If chalkos is read strictly as the alloy bronze, then pure copper Cu is also never named in its elemental form in the Odyssey; it is only met as the undifferentiated chalkos. On the looser literary shorthand chalkos = copper/bronze, copper is present only as the alloy.

Non-metals:
Theion sulphur and carbon/charcoal are raised. Theion is not a Homeric word in the elemental sense; carbon is indirectly referenced via charcoal/soot, e.g. Od. 18.175-176, 22.455-456, so it is generally excluded from the omission list.

Current stable belief:
Au and Ag are definitely named. Sn and Hg are definitely not named. Fe and Pb are effectively absent from the Odyssey in any secure elemental naming, with strong scholarly argument for their absence. Cu is ambiguous because of chalkos/bronze.

Unresolved questions:
Exact Odyssey attestations of sideros and molybdos vs Iliad-only usage, and whether chalkos should be counted as a naming of pure copper. Whether the question wants the strict elemental inventory Cu, Sn, Pb, Fe, Hg un-named with Au, Ag named, or the canonical minimal set Sn, Hg, with Pb/Fe marginal, or lead/tin/mercury as per Colleague 10/7.

reflection_text.4:

Secure unanimous attestations in the Odyssey:
* chrysos = Au gold, ubiquitous e.g. Od. 4.73, 7.86-87, 7.129, 8.397
* argyros = Ag silver, ubiquitous with gold
* chalkos = the Heroic Age working metal, weapons, fittings, cauldrons e.g. Od. 9.383 ff, 14.334, 21.11. In Homer chalkos is an undifferentiated Cu-Sn alloy, bronze; the two modern constituents are never isolated and named.

Uncontested absences by name:
* Sn tin. Greek kassiteros/kassiteron is a post-Homeric loan, 5th c. and later. Tin is physically present in chalkos but never isolated and named in Iliad or Odyssey. This is the canonical Homeric tin lacuna.
* Hg mercury/quicksilver. Hydrargyros/hydrargos ‘liquid silver’ is post-Homeric technical terminology. No elemental mercury is named in the epics.

Disputed / marginal cases:
* Fe iron / sideros. Colleagues 6,7,8 cite Od. 9.391, 15.xxx etc. as attestations; colleagues 1,2,4,5,9 treat sideros as essentially Iliadic, marginal/exoticising in the Odyssey, the poem being a Bronze Age epic. Current leaning: effectively absent/marginal in the Odyssey proper.
* Pb lead / molybdos/molybdaina. Colleagues 4,8,9 cite molybdos for weights/sinkers e.g. Od. 21.11; colleagues 1,2,5,6 argue molybdos is post-Homeric and no secure elemental lead name occurs in the Odyssey. Status remains disputed, with most treating lead as effectively un-named in the poem’s metal vocabulary.
* Cu copper. On a strict elemental reading copper is never named pure, only as the alloy chalkos/bronze. On a looser literary reading chalkos is taken as ‘copper/bronze’. This reading affects whether Cu counts as mentioned.

Carbon is referenced indirectly via charcoal/anthrax and soot in smithing/cooking contexts, e.g. Od. 18.175-176, 22.455-456, so it is present in narrative terms. Sulfur/theion is never named elementally.

That trio therefore gives the most consistent and textbook-accurate statement of the gaps.

The Odyssey’s own metal nomenclature is the gold-silver-bronze nomenclature of the
late Bronze / early Iron Age Aegean.

* chrysos = Au is named again and again, Od. 4.73, 7.86-87, 7.129, 8.397 etc.
* argyros = Ag is named with it, Od. 7.86-87, 7.129, 4.73 etc.
* chalkos / khalkos is the normal Homeric working metal, weapons, fittings,
tripods, cauldrons, Od. 9.383 ff., 14.334, 21.11 etc. In Homeric usage
chalkos is the single material substance we call bronze, the Cu-Sn alloy.
It is never analysed into its two modern pure constituents.

On the classical seven ancient metals that were already handled in the
Eastern Mediterranean c. 800 BCE

Au Ag Cu Sn Pb Fe Hg

Zn and Sb being explicitly excluded as not fully recognised in elemental
form, the poem therefore names Au and Ag by unambiguous elemental name
and it names bronze/chalkos as a material.

The textbook Homeric gaps are the components of that bronze and the
liquid metal.

* Sn tin. The Greek name kassiteros/kassiteron ‘tin’ is a post-Homeric
loan, 5th c. and later. Tin is physically present in Homeric bronze but
the metal is never isolated and named in the Iliad or the Odyssey.
Bronze is always chalkos, a single material for Homer. That is the
normal Homeric tin lacuna.

* Hg mercury / quicksilver. Hydrargyros/hydrargos ‘liquid silver’ is a
post-Homeric technical term. No Homeric passage names a liquid silver
or a separate mercury metal as an element.

That is the uncontroversial core. On the same strict elemental naming
criterion the Odyssey has no normal elemental name for lead and in
practice no normal elemental name for iron either.

epics. The few ‘molybd-’ loci that are quoted are late glosses and the
poem has no secure elemental lead name in its own metal nomenclature.
Lead is one of the three classical metals already in routine use in the
8th c. Mediterranean which is without any unambiguous elemental mention
in the Odyssey.

* Fe sideros ‘iron’ is the rare, exoticising word of the Iliad. In the
Odyssey it is at best a very marginal, late survival and the epic’s
technology remains a bronze technology. For the Odyssey proper iron is
effectively un-named as a normal working metal.

If chalkos is read strictly as the alloy bronze and not as pure copper,
pure Cu is also never isolated and named in the poem, it is only met in
the undifferentiated alloy chalkos. On the usual literary shorthand that

reflection_text.4:
The discussion is converging on a gold-silver-bronze lexicon for the Odyssey and an ~8th c. BCE known-elemental repertoire of Au Ag Cu Sn Pb Fe Hg, Zn and Sb excluded.

Secure unanimous attestations in the Odyssey:
* chrysos = Au gold, ubiquitous e.g. Od. 4.73, 7.86-87, 7.129, 8.397
* argyros = Ag silver, ubiquitous with gold
* chalkos = the Heroic Age working metal, weapons, fittings, cauldrons e.g. Od. 9.383 ff, 14.334, 21.11. In Homer chalkos is an undifferentiated Cu-Sn alloy, bronze; the two modern constituents are never isolated and named.

Uncontested absences by name:
* Sn tin. Greek kassiteros/kassiteron is a post-Homeric loan, 5th c. and later. Tin is physically present in chalkos but never isolated and named in Iliad or Odyssey. This is the canonical Homeric tin lacuna.
* Hg mercury/quicksilver. Hydrargyros/hydrargos ‘liquid silver’ is post-Homeric technical terminology. No elemental mercury is named in the epics.

Disputed / marginal cases, now narrowing:
* Fe iron / sideros. Most round-2 contributors treat sideros as essentially Iliadic, marginal/exoticising in the Odyssey, the poem being a Bronze Age epic. A few citations Od. 9.391 etc. are mentioned but the consensus is iron is at best rare/absent as a normal working metal in the Odyssey proper.

Round-2 weight is shifting to absence: molybdos in the elemental sense is treated as post-Homeric and there is no secure elemental lead name in the Odyssey’s own metal nomenclature. Colleagues 7 and 10 now explicitly place lead in the clean omission set with tin and mercury.
* Cu copper. On a strict elemental reading copper is never named pure, only as the alloy chalkos/bronze. On a looser literary reading chalkos is taken as ‘copper/bronze’. This reading affects whether Cu counts as mentioned.

Non-metals / incidental:
Carbon is referenced indirectly via charcoal/anthrax and soot in smithing/cooking contexts, e.g. Od. 18.175-176, 22.455-456, so colleagues 10/7 treat carbon as present in narrative terms and not an omission. Sulfur/theion is never named elementally.

Synthesis after round 2:
The minimal uncontested core remains Au and Ag unambiguously named, chalkos for bronze, with Sn and Hg as the textbook canonical un-named classical metals. The expanded practical consensus now commonly adds Pb lead as securely absent by name in the Odyssey, and Fe iron as effectively absent/marginal in the Odyssey proper. Mediterranean without an elemental name in the Odyssey, with carbon excluded via charcoal. 10.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: The convergence in round 2 around lead, tin and mercury as the clean, textbook set of omissions now looks decisive. All the classical seven metals except gold and silver are absent from the Odyssey’s elemental vocabulary, but the three that receive no lexical mention whatsoever—molybdos for lead, kassiteros for tin, and hydrargyros for mercury—are the clearest gaps, since each was already handled as a distinct native substance in the eighth-century Mediterranean. Charcoal (anthrax) and soot are repeatedly named as practical substances in smithing and household scenes (Od. 18.175–176, 22.455–456), so carbon cannot be placed on the same omission list; it is already present in the poem’s own practical terminology. Sideros remains marginal at best—essentially an Iliadic word and at most an exoticising rarity in the Odyssey—so it does not belong with the stricter lacunae. The minimal, most consistent statement of the elements known in elemental form by the time of composition yet never named in the poem is therefore simply lead, tin and mercury.

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: The emerging consensus on lead, tin and mercury as the three classical metals already in routine eighth-century Mediterranean use but lacking any unambiguous elemental name in the Odyssey itself remains the cleanest and most textually grounded formulation. The repeated practical mentions of charcoal (anthrax) and soot in smithing and household scenes already place carbon squarely within the poem’s recognized substances, so it cannot be counted among the omissions. Iron stays marginal at best—an essentially Iliadic term that appears only in exoticising or late contexts in the Odyssey and never functions as a normal working metal. Copper is present only as the undifferentiated alloy chalkos, which the poem never analyses into its modern constituents. By contrast, the post-Homeric character of molybdos, kassiteros and hydrargyros is secure, and each metal was demonstrably handled in native form by the time the epic took shape. That trio therefore supplies the most consistent statement of the elemental gaps attested by the poem’s own vocabulary.

10.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: The round-3 convergence on lead, tin and mercury as the clean set of omissions now looks decisive and fully consistent with the poem’s own lexical evidence. The classical metals already handled in elemental form by the eighth-century Mediterranean are Au, Ag, Cu, Sn, Pb, Fe and Hg; the Odyssey names only Au and Ag unambiguously and uses chalkos for the undifferentiated Cu-Sn alloy, never isolating pure copper. Kassiteros, molybdos and hydrargyros are all post-Homeric technical terms, so tin, lead and mercury—each demonstrably used as native substances by the time of composition—receive no elemental name in the text. Charcoal (anthrax) and soot appear repeatedly in smithing and household scenes (Od. 18.175–176, 22.455–456), placing a recognised carbonaceous material squarely inside the poem’s practical vocabulary and therefore excluding carbon from the omission list.
